credit.video_title: Anthropic’s Market Debut And What Comes Next For NVIDIA | November mARKet Update

sentences.en: Hello and welcome to the November 2026 market update webinar.
My name is Dan White, one of ARC's portfolio managers, and I will be moderating today's call.
This call was pre-recorded on November 16th, 2026.
With that, I'll now turn it over to ARC's CEO and CIO, Kathy Wood.
Kathy.
Okay, Dan, thank you.
My how the world has changed.
The election happened and the market is very unsettled by lots of news, not the least of which is the drama with Nvidia.
But before we get there, and we will get there very quickly, I'd like to just give a few thoughts about where we believe we are now, especially relative to my last in the no.
So we do know that the Fed is commenting more and more often contrary to our expectations about inflation and concerns about inflation and therefore interest rates going up.
This has unsettled the market.
This is not what we expected from a wash fed.

But it is happening and I think the reason he's shall I say allowing it maybe even encouraging it to some extent is because the diffusion index for the PCE deflator that inflation rate or that diffusion index has hooked

Up in here and I do think it is because of energy prices going up and feeding into many categories of goods and services now especially goods who have that have to be transported from point A to point B
And therefore rely on diesel oil.
So it is diffusing a bit but many of the indicators we are watching are doing the opposite.
I think the most important indicator is gold.
sentences.zh: 我認為最重要的指標是黃金。

sentences.en: The gold price has dropped roughly 31% 30-ish percent since the since the president appointed chairman Worsh as chairman.
Now I know from his past that Chairman Worsh feels very strongly about the gold price.
In fact, as strongly as Greenspan and Vulkar did, I believe.
Both of them seem to manage monetary policy according to the gold price.
sentences.zh: 他們兩位似乎都是依照金價來調整貨幣政策。

sentences.en: So I do believe that Chairman Worsh feels that we are licking inflation.
But he wants to make sure and so this diffusion index meaning the percentage of prices increasing at 3% or faster on a year-over-year basis.
He wants to see that move back down from the a little above 50% back down actually to around 30 to 35%.
And so that's one thing.
The other thing that or the other point that I'd like to make here about Chairman Worsh is about productivity.
We got an excellent productivity number in the last quarter.
sentences.zh: 上一季我們拿到了非常亮眼的生產力數字。

sentences.en: It was 3.6% at an annual rate from the second to the third quarter.
And more important unit labor costs declined.
sentences.zh: 更重要的是，單位勞動成本下降了。

sentences.en: They actually went negative.
So down 0.7% from the second quarter to third quarter.
I know that chairman Worsh watches those variables very carefully as well.
And so I do believe he believes that inflation will be coming down.
sentences.zh: 所以我確實相信，他認為通膨將會下降。

sentences.en: He just wants to make sure that this diesel price increase and energy price increase generally does not diffuse much more through other areas of goods and services in the deflator and then speaking of oil we have already a
15% drop roughly from the peak and as I mentioned in the no and in the letter I wrote recently we are seeing a burgeoning of oil production in the Middle East.
Now it's still hemmed in a bit by the conflict there.
But we believe that Saudi Arabia and the UAE are starting to pump oil aggressively in anticipation of the strait opening up again.
But also for another important reason.
I think both of them think that the oil price has peaked now.
sentences.zh: 我認為他們兩位都覺得油價現在已經見頂了。

sentences.en: It truly peaked in '08 at 147 dollars per barrel.
And then it peaked again after CO or during COVID and again recently I think it just hit the COVID level as well.
And I think they're taking their cues from actually innovation.
May be reading our research because we do believe that transportation is move moving onto the grid.
Transportation of all kinds so cars, trucks, drones, we're now seeing Walmart work with zipline to allow very fast drone deliveries.
And we think that's going to that that's going to spread throughout the United States pretty quickly.
But we know that 57% of oil consumption is transportation and if it starts moving off the grid then the Middle East has lost a big customer.
And so we believe they understand that especially because they are focused on autonomous mobility themselves.

So, we've got the ingredients of a significant drop in inflation in place, we believe, and we've got a very important leading indicator, the gold price, telling us or confirming that we're probably going to see a significant drop in
Inflation.
This market is depending importantly on that and the last few inflation indicators have been unsettling because the Fed is so focused on this diffusion index.
So we'll we believe within the next few months this will resolve quickly.
And of course that does depend as it has all year on a resolution of the conflict in the Middle East.
We do think we're getting closer.
We're also getting a little closer in Ukraine, Russia as well.
So it's darkest before the dawn.
sentences.zh: 所以說，黎明前總是最黑暗的。

sentences.en: And I do think that a lot of investors have attributed the election results and the re recent inflation indicators as reasons to sell the market.
Now on election results, what do we think there?
I think we're looking at gridlock.
sentences.zh: 我認為我們會看到（政治）僵局。

sentences.en: President Trump still does have veto power and will need twothirds of both houses or both the House and the Senate to override those vetos.
That will be very difficult even with the landslide that the Democrats enjoyed in this last election.
So for the next two years, I don't think we'll see huge changes.
sentences.zh: 所以未來兩年，我不認為會有什麼巨大的改變。

sentences.en: I do think the market is beginning to wonder what will happen post 28 election.
So in 29 and we have some time to figure that out.

Of course, the most important thing about innovation though, and what we're going to be watching most closely, whether it's AI or crypto or autonomous mobility, is are consumers and businesses being delighted by this innovation?
And a good lesson for us, was very early on with Uber.
I was living and Ark was in well, Ark may not have been born when Uber was born, but whether at my last firm or at Ark, we were thinking about Uber trying to get through the New York taxi
Commission, the New York City Taxi Commission.
And we thought that would be a tall order.
What Uber did was just blast right through New York.
Why?
Because it was delighting consumers.
And we think AI and crypto and autonomous mobility will in many ways delight consumers you know better, faster, cheaper, more productive, more efficient, more creative products and services.
So stay tuned.
We have not given up.
We think that we are at the dawn of a technology revolution.
sentences.zh: 我們認為我們正處於一場科技革命的開端。

sentences.en: This is not the tech and telecom bubble and bust.
We are climbing a massive wall of worry here and we've just put a few more bricks in with the election and with Fed rhetoric.
But we do think the resolution of this is on the bull side of the equation.
Great.
Thank you Kathy.
But before we dive into the usual Q&A portion of today's webinar, we're going to start with a, you know, just question up front.
And this is an evolving situation at NVIDIA.
I want to remind listeners again, this conversation was recorded on November 16th, so more information might come out by the time of this release.
But Kathy, Frank, you know, based on what we know today, what are you thinking and how has the Nvidia investment thesis changed?
Yeah, I'm happy to start and feel free to add in Kathy.
I think you know of course it's a very unfortunate situation not just for Nvidia but investors and the world watching what's going on in AI right now.

And I think when we try to think of what what's actually changing on the ground and I should caveat similar to you Dan what is actually known because there's a lot of rumors and allegations and the facts are
Still very early and coming out.

When we look at Nvidia and what the implications could be, I think there's the standard things with a unexpected CEO transition where you have often heightened execution risk, a pullback in the company's multiple as the market tries to
Understand what those risks could be and what the magnitude are.
But specific to Nvidia, I think there's a few things.
One is, Jensen was notorious for, you know, managing the company, in a very flat way with 60 direct reports.
He really had an iron grip on a lot of what was going on at the company.
So, those are big shoes to fill.
sentences.zh: 所以，那是很難接替的位置（很難有人比得上）。

sentences.en: And there's not a clear su successor inside the company.
And I should mention also that, you know, as of well, we're recording, there's a petition signed by 180 plus thousand employees and investors and the general public.
Trying to bring Jensen back.
We will see what happens there.
But in addition to that Jensen had a very strong control over the semiconductor supply chain.

Famously making handshake deals in Taiwan and whining and dining various leaders in the semiconductor industry to procure as much forward capacity for Nvidia as possible which allowed them to deliver excellent results and also restrict their competition from getting
The supply they would need to gain as much share as they otherwise would have.
So, whoever fills those shoes will likely not have relationships as strong as Jensen does or did.

And then another implication is possibly what led to all of these allegations coming to light which is increasing restrictions on chip sales not just into China directly but also to the broader Asia region where we have seen this
Kind of growing industry of companies that are exploiting an open looole loophole in the export restrictions which allow companies to sit in areas such as Singapore and Malaysia.
Take the latest generation Nvidia chips and then on rent them into China.
Now there's allegations that they were e illicitly shipping them directly into China but even outside of that renting the compute to companies in China.
We've already seen some moves by the administration that this is likely to be cracked down on which could create you know at minimum a need to divert those sales to regions like the US and Europe.
Of which Nvidia is probably the most exposed to.
So those are some of the things that we're watching here.
And again very rapidly evolving situation.
Yeah.
And I just add one thing.
Talent.
There's a voracious appetite for talent and invid Nvidia's engineers are cream of the crop.
So that's another consideration here.
The longer there's a vacuum the more tempted talent will be to move to really attractive offers out there.
That that's one.
So let's see how long this lasts.
And then of course I mean we do have the president of Sam Alman and OpenAI and all of that.
You know 186,000 did you say something like that signatures including Elon Musk who wanted to publicize that he had he had signed the petition.
You've got Treasury Secretary Bessant basically saying the government's going to get involved and everything has to change.
The board has to change, the management has to everything has to change.

You've got President Trump on the other hand say you know Jensen built an amazing company and you know he's a really good guy and we don't believe that you know that he was will be implicated in this scandal.
So I think that that's another layer of uncertainty you know in terms of the government getting involved.
Definitely.

And the so yeah if I just add one last thing which is implications for the broader ecosystem around Nvidia because and I think Jensen was leading the charge and in fact we've seen reporting that Colette Crest the CFO

Who's taking over as interim CFO may have buted heads with Jensen over this is Nvidia's support for the Neocloud ecosystem the startup ecosystem open source as well and Nvidia generating so much free cash flow today was really reinvesting

It back into the ecosystem and it's likely that whoever does take over if it's not Jensen will be more conservative in the least in how they allocate that capital and one other thing because that is where the circular

Argument oh this is just like the tech and telecom bubble so shortterm yes some reverberations for sure and we have to address coreweave we own coreweave anyone who listened to coreweave's call understands what a great management team cororeweave

Has how well they've thought through the risks here and I think the most important piece of information that we've received from Core's management is you know they are insisting upon pre prepayments and they've been getting them.
Most people had assumed that they were getting them they were giving they were getting them and the exchange was a discount.
There have been no discounts recently.

So very tight supply demand and coreweave is platinum rated by what is it semi analysis semi-analysis and Nebius is I think as well but coreweave's quarter was far superior to Nebius's if I if I remember correctly.
Yeah, I think I think Nebius had a more cautious demand picture in the near term.
I think the opportunity is large for both these companies.
sentences.zh: 我認為這兩家公司的機會都很大。

sentences.en: But I think you know we saw really clear signals of the followrough in GPU pricing going into their long-term contracts strength in the short-term contracts.
The difference between those about 20 to 25 billion for new long-term contracts and $40 billion per gigawatt for the short term.
So they're building a portfolio of both of these deal structures.

And then also you know a lot of reporting goes into their longerdated maturity corporate level bonds and they're going to be able to fund the next wave of the buildout without doing more parent company level debt financing and
Instead leveraging the assetbacked lending plus the prepayments that you mentioned.
Right.
Right.
So what we've what we know so far and what's still kind of up in the air, there's still a lot of hair on this.
Have you made any adjustments to like the ARC scoring system?
Yes.
So we evaluate companies on a variety of dimensions.
sentences.zh: 所以我們從多個面向來評估公司。

sentences.en: One of them is the people management and culture.
Another one is thesis risk.
And we have even if Jensen were to come back he will not have the same influence as he had previously.

And so we've taken down our people management and culture score and we've increased thesis risk because of the normal things like execution risk with a management turnover risks to losing talent and then also the increased risk of government
Intervention.

Now one other thing we should note is right now Nvidia has roughly 83% of the GPU market roughly very high and we have battle tested share losses that was our first thought okay other companies are going to become
More aggressive and we'll have more success here to the tune of taking it from 83 to 38%.

Now, all other things equal and all other things are not equal, of course, that would over a five-year period still given the rate at which we think AI is going to expand and permeate every sector, every industry, every
Company.
That still would have delivered a 25% compound annual rate of return.
However, the question is in the valuation now.
And I think we even had the valuation the terminal valuation at a discount to the past 10 years.
But it could be even below that.
It could be below I think it was 26 times EV to EBIDA roughly 25 26.

I remember the days long time ago when Nvidia was just a PC gaming chip company and it sold at 10 times and I remember we were pounding the table because of autonomous mobility and AI generally back then.
So that was a very good call.
I doubt I doubt we'll ever see anything close to 10.
But could it go down from 25 if the government causes it a lot of trouble?
Sure it could.
Yeah.
And we're talking the long-term average.
It's depressed and below the average market and closer to that right now.
But in a normal market, we expect it'd be priced differently.
Yes.
Yes.
All right.
I'm sure there's still a lot more to come on Nvidia.
I would guess it's another question next month.
And you know, I think you said at the beginning as well, there's by the time this comes out, a lot more news could come out and even earnings are tomorrow night as well.
So you know we we'll be keeping investors attuned on our thesis here.
We will now begin the regular question and answer portion of today's webinar.
sentences.zh: 現在我們要開始今天網路研討會的例行問答環節。

sentences.en: Questions were received from our clients distribution partners and sent to our funds X and Instagram accounts at ARC_F funs.
The first question Kathy we're coming right back to you.
Is rising interest rates still an effective way to fight inflation in today's economy or does it amplify the affordability problem?

You know, we were just in our economics meeting and talking about this topic and I do remember the difference between the 70s today and I remember this really through my parents and the decisions they were making.
We lived in Southern California, real estate was a big deal, still is a big deal.
And the psych psychology back then was so different from the psychology today.
Back then, housing was booming.
Why?
Because it was considered an inflation hedge.
sentences.zh: 因為它被視為對抗通膨的避險工具。

sentences.en: And prospective homeowners and existing homeowners basically were they were buying as soon as they could in order to avoid paying even higher interest rates.
So there was this inflationary mentality and the reason they were willing to buy is because home prices were going up so much faster than the level of interest rates.
So that was the psychology back then.
sentences.zh: 所以那就是當時的心態。

sentences.en: A very different psychology right now.
We have people trapped in their homes, right?
Trapped in their homes.
Because their existing mortgage rate is let's say 2 to 3% something around there.
And the one they'd have to pay is closer to 7%.
Just not affordable.
So from a housing point of view we're talking about supply demand imbalance like you know we've never seen people want to sell but they can't move.
So it's a completely different psychology and I think I think we need to remember that.

In our recent letter and in the and recent in the no, we focused on interest rates going up not because of inflation because interestingly the bond market is basically saying the recent increase in yield is more because of
Real growth expectations than inflation expectations.
sentences.zh: （看的是）實質成長預期，而不是通膨預期。

sentences.en: And now that's changed a little bit recently.
But still by and large that is what the bond market thinks.
So if the real economy is not going to be derailed by rising rates then I think I think we don't have as much of an issue as we did during COVID.
So during COVID and the supply chain bottlenecks we were facing there interest rates going up basically shut down the real economy.
Manufacturing sector was declining, housing sector declined, small business declined.
sentences.zh: 製造業在衰退，房市衰退，小型企業也衰退。

sentences.en: If we're right and we are in a technology revolution that will not be derailed by the drama at Nvidia and we don't think it will.
Why?
Because of this delighting the consumer and business.
You know, I think that is really happening.
We can just look at ARC how delighted many people are by getting rid of all the drudgery work they had to do and really enjoying their careers even more.
So I think the more that continues the stronger this revolution is going to get and this is all from a if I had to reflect on the tech and telecom bubble days I was a young portfolio manager back

Then there were there wasn't a wall of worry there was in fact it was quite the opposite it was Y2K okay because of Y2K technology spending is going to just continue booming and so very different environment then versus
Now because many people do compare this to the tech and telecom bubble.
No, this is the real deal.
This is the technology revolution we've been waiting for since the seeds were planted in the 20 years that ended in the tech and telecom bubble.
Okay, they have been germinating.
They're flourishing now.
And I really do believe that the big surprises ahead are going to be to the upside.

But in the meantime, because of this fear, I think that any speculative excess that was starting to occur, let's say ordering more chips than a company really needed just to try and get ahead of the next company.
We're going to see that die down, which is a risk to Nvidia and the chip company short term, right?
But I don't think it will be long lasting because this AI revolution is real.
sentences.zh: 但我不認為它會持續很久，因為這場 AI 革命是真的。

sentences.en: We see it daytoday in our businesses and in our personal lives.
And on the growth side too I would say real growth and I think we all agree is much higher than I think most people are considering it to be.
And if that housing side like you said turns back on that's just some more fuel you know that an economic multiplier that's just more fuel to real growth.
Yes.
So manufacturing has just started to come back in a big way this year.
I would say helped along by AI, but it's broadening out to be sure.
And yes, we've had no help from housing.
None.
And housing I think has as big a multiplier for the economy as capital spending has.
And I'll remind our viewers, we really do believe that 3.4% real GDP growth in the third quarter was not a fluke.
It was productivity driven.
And we think we're going to see a lot more productivity, which is going to drive real GDP growth to much higher levels than anyone now expects.
We're thinking seven to eight% in the fiveyear t five to 10 year time horizon.
7 to 9% I should say.
Nobody believes that's possible, but we think we're already on our way.
So very different from the supply chain issues during COVID and the interest rate increases then, very different from the tech and telecom bubble.
So I think any settling down of the spec inventory speculation will be good for the sustainability of this cycle and those growth numbers.
I think sometimes we say and people can look at us like we have two heads because they're so large.
But you talk to these tech leaders like an Elon or a Dario who are seeing this AI proliferate in their companies and the uplift that they have and they're actually higher than we are.
Yes.
And so who knows maybe we end up being conservative on that measure.
Yeah.
Well, I think Elon's is somewhere in the 20 to 30% GDP growth range.
Yes, we're more conservative than Elon.
sentences.zh: 對，我們比 Elon 保守。

sentences.en: All right.
Into our second question here.
Kathy, I'll stay with you on kind of the high level side here.
So with a divided Washington, which areas of innovation face the most policy change and which are least exposed?
Well, Tasha Daniel and I just were at the Kennedy Space Center last week, and I can't tell you how bipartisan this space revolution is.
Everybody is excited about it.
Both parties.
And of course Starship the ship of Starship being caught in chopsticks yesterday was or yesterday meaning Saturday, right?
Saturday this past Saturday.
Just unbelievable.
We're living through an incredible again technology revolution.
That's proof positive of it.
So space I think is bipartisan.
sentences.zh: 所以我認為太空是兩黨都支持的議題。

sentences.en: Energy has become more bipartisan particularly nuclear energy.

I think that's been the biggest shift over the last 10 15 years is even the environmentalists are now looking and analyzing nuclear through a different lens of some sort because I think that has become bipartisan.
And I do believe what I said before in terms of delighting consumers, delighting businesses to the extent that happens in the next two years while we're in gridlock.
And actually we have more than two years because the new administration won't be in until early 29.

To the extent consumers and businesses find all of these new technologies to be delightful then I think that the partisanship around them historically crypto to some extent AI to some extent EVs and autonomous vehicles I think we've hit
Escape velocity on that one because both Tesla now and Whimo are saying we have surpassed meaning autonomous vehicles have surpassed human-driven vehicles in safety.
So regulators are probably going to climb on board around the world.
sentences.zh: 所以全世界的監管機關大概都會跟進。

sentences.en: They'll be forced to safer than humans at some point.
Yes.
Frank, we're going to come to you.
I you know I think I could say every week is a big week in AI but with anthropic coming to public I think it's justified to say this is a big week in your AI world.
So what does a public enthropic mean for venture capitalist valuing private rounds of AI companies?
Yeah I I'll speak about this generally just making sense of the anthropic valuation and also you know talking about private assets.
We're happy to have Anthropic as the top five, the number five name in our venture fund right now.
And are happy for it to be accessible in the public markets for the other funds that may be interested.
And you know how we make sense of the valuation.
The high end of the range for Anthropic would imply a 1.4 trillion valuation.
They updated their S1 last week and noted that their October ending ARR was 81 billion.
That's the annualized run rate revenue.
And if you were to compare that to public market comps, that's about a 17 times multiple on rate revenue.

If you're going to do the same analysis for some of the highest priced public software companies that are really deemed the AI winners in the market, you have Palunteer, Cloudflare, and Crowd Strike as those three highest valuation companies
In the public software market.
They're all priced at 30 times forward sales plus.
So in that perspective, you would say Anthropic looks pretty reasonably priced.
And I think even more so when you factor in that Anthropic is growing mid to high triple digits versus those companies mid to high double digits on revenue.
Anthropic really is a company growing at a rate and a scale that we have never seen before outside of what probably OpenAI is doing.
So I think that helps put the valuation into context.
sentences.zh: 所以我認為這有助於把估值放在整體脈絡中來看。

sentences.en: Of course the debate is over whether that growth rate will continue or that revenue could continue to grow, our research suggests it will.
I think we're very early in tapping this knowledge work opportunity which is $40 trillion of global wages.
And so while we'll have kind of not a smooth ramp, you know, this is usage based billing primarily.
So you have fluctuations in growth rate that the market likes to run wild with.
sentences.zh: 所以成長率會有波動，而市場很喜歡拿這個大做文章。

sentences.en: I think overall the opportunity for this company is very much still to come as they enter the public markets.
And of course it's a comparison point for other investors especially those that invest across the public and private markets.

I think coinciding OpenAI's round with Anthropics round and if you just compare the two valuations which are relatively similar, Anthropics round may be impacting why OpenAI it looks like didn't fill out the full target that they set out
To raise.
Great.
Thank you, Frank.
We're going to stay with you for more AI.
So if AI inference costs are falling as fast as we've seen, if they continue to, does this help or hurt the companies that are selling these models, that usage plan?
Yes, good question.
Of course, a hot topic.
I think it's important to re recognize that cost declines are inherent to innovative technologies.
If we didn't see cost declines, I think that actually would be a signal for concern versus otherwise.
So I think that's really important.
In AI, we've seen extremely strong and consistent cost declines.
sentences.zh: 在 AI 領域，我們看到成本下降得非常強勁而且持續。

sentences.en: You can actually go all the way back to 2012 kind of the advent of deep learning.
Open eye published research on this back in 2020.
So going back a ways you could see the purely from software efficiencies not including hardware improvement the cost to train AI models was falling about 50% per year.
So all else equal even if you don't have any new hardware advances you have this underlying cost decline inherent in artificial intelligence.
And that does flow through to lower unit prices.
And you're getting more intelligence per dollar.
That's a good thing.
It unlocks new pockets of demand and makes new use cases possible.
sentences.zh: 它釋放出新的需求，也讓新的應用情境成為可能。

sentences.en: We've seen how these new units can be used in ways that I think are hard to comprehend until you see the innovation.
One example is going from traditional models to reasoning models.
They stop to think before they answer consumes maybe 10 times more tokens, but you get a much better answer.
I think the next examples of those agents has been another one.
The next examples are going to be the persistent agents that are working for you even when you're not asking it a direct question.
That's like Grockbot, Metas, Muse, OpenAI, and Anthropic each have their versions of it.
And particularly for the hard sciences, you're going to have a multi- aent systems.
Anthrop OpenAI used a 100,000 agent multi- aent system to solve the Millennium Prize problem that consumes a lot of tokens, but it does things that were not possible previously.
So I think we should expect cost declines and unit prices to continue going down.
sentences.zh: 所以我認為我們應該預期成本和單價會繼續下降。

sentences.en: But look at what the value of what's unlocked and how the diffusion of the technology is enabled because of those cost declines.
One last thing what signals can we look at to see if the supply of tokens is overwhelming the demand.
You can look at the company earnings.
We're going to have anthropic reporting quarterly.
I mentioned ARR is now 81 billion for them.
It was 71 billion at the end of September.
So they added 10 billion in run rate revenue.
The continued revenue growth of open eye and anthropic is a signal to watch as well as some of the more real-time platforms like spending on open router and spending on ramp.
They both have dashboards where you can track this and there we have seen open router spend kind of leveling off.
Ramp spend there looks like there's some digestion as well.
But this coincides with new model releases that come out with a lower price.
Businesses instantly get a break in their spending.
sentences.zh: 企業的支出立刻就減輕了。

sentences.en: But then you see Jevans paradox kick in and revenue growth accelerates out the back end.
And I expect that we'll continue to see those occurring over time.
Yeah.
So I'd like to just clarify something.
You said 50% that was their 2020 study opening.
Yeah.
I think our audience is used to that 75% number.
75% per year drop in training costs.
99% per year drop in inference cost.
How much it costs these models to answer our question.
Yeah, exactly.
That OpenAI study was looking at purely software.
So you get about a 50% cost reduction from software.
The hardware also gets about 2x better every year.
So you get a 50% cost decline on hardware.
So you combine the two, that's the 75% total cost reduction in training.
And then yes, inference has been falling even more quickly.
Yeah.
And I I'd like to add a couple of points as it relates to inflation as well.
You know, a lot of people are focused on the memory cost explosion.

So OID, how do base editing, prime editing, and what we tend to hear a lot about a lot is just the crisper editing, how do those compare, and does ARC have a clear winner?
Thanks, Dan.
I wouldn't really say it's a question of which one wins.
Each of these are all different tools and the right choice depends on the disease the edit and the cells that you know the intervention is trying to reach.
Every gene editor needs to find a target in some DNA and change it cut it and re ideally repair it and fix it.
Crisper made this targeting programmable and easier.
And the differences is how these changes get made.
You can think of classic crisper like a pair of scissors, base editing like a pencil, and prime editing more like a word processor.
So, classic crisper cuts both strands of DNA.
And as the cell repairs the cuts, it introduces some small changes.
And that's actually a really effective way for disrupting a d a gene or knocking it out or knocking it down so that it's no longer, you know, affecting the cell and the patient.
It's also the most clinically established.
So, CASJVI, which is a FDI approved treatment for cickle cell, uses a classic crisper approach and is the first crisper-based gene editing medicine that's been approved.
The trade-off is you get a little bit less control over exactly how that repair happens.
And so, you can get a mix of small insertions and deletions and sometimes you can get some unwanted DNA changes.
So, it's powerful.
It's a powerful tool for disrupting the gene.
But precise corrections can require additional machinery.

If you take base editing it changes the individual it changes individual DNA nucleotides without deliberately breaking both the strands and this matters because single letter substitutions account for roughly half of the catal of the catalog disease-causing genetic variants
Today.
The trade-off is that established base editors, they only make certain DNA changes and they can also edit some of the some of the adjacent nucleotides as well.
And so but these the these are also in the clinic with companies with companies like Beam using this technology.
Prime editing is really about search and replace.
It can make it can make all the different DNA substitutions plus small insertions and deletions again without the double stranded break.
So offering kind of more flexibility and also less likelihood of a kind of offtarget or unwanted or unwanted effects.

So, looking across them, they are they're all useful for different contexts, depending on whether you want to just knock down a gene, whether you want to make a small correction or a large correction.
And, and the other challenge is really not just the type of editing, but the type of delivery used, you know, to get it to various places in the body.
So we think all of them will have a place and many of the technologies are already progressing into the clinic.
